bill.title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States relating to contributions and expenditures intended to affect elections.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
bill.officialSummary: This joint resolution proposes a constitutional amendment authorizing Congress and the states to set reasonable limits on the raising and spending of money by candidates and others to influence elections. The amendment grants Congress and the states the power to implement and enforce this amendment by legislation. They are allowed to distinguish between natural persons and corporations or other artificial entities created by law, including by prohibiting such entities from spending money to influence elections.

classification.plainSummary: This joint resolution proposes a constitutional amendment that would allow Congress and state governments to set limits on how much money candidates and others can raise and spend to influence elections. It would also permit lawmakers to treat corporations and other legal entities differently from individual people, including by banning corporate spending on elections. The amendment would require ratification by the states to take effect.

industries.rationale: Campaign finance regulation directly affects lobbying firms and election-law practitioners who advise on contribution and expenditure compliance.
Advocacy organizations that spend money on election-related communications would face new regulatory constraints on their expenditures.
Limits on campaign spending could affect demand for political advertising across broadcast, digital, and print media platforms.
Financial institutions that make political expenditures or operate PACs could face new restrictions on corporate election spending.

plain.whatItDoes: This joint resolution would propose a constitutional amendment authorizing Congress and the states to set reasonable limits on the raising and spending of money by candidates and others to influence elections.
plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who deals with a federal agency.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in dealing with the government. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: Reworded from the official summary. Staff at the Congressional Research Service wrote that summary. It is public domain, and the full text of it is further down this page.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
